cues.text: Saul of Tarsus
Paul was born a Jew of the Diaspora at Tarsus in Cilicia, and inherited from his family the prized status of Roman citizen.
Sent to Jerusalem, he studied the Law under the great rabbi Gamaliel and became a zealous Pharisee, earning his bread, in the fashion of the rabbis, as a tentmaker.
His zeal turned him into a fierce enemy of the new sect of the Nazarenes: he consented to the stoning of St.
Stephen and set out to hunt down the Christians of Damascus.
The Road to Damascus
On that road, about midday, a light from heaven struck him to the ground, and a voice said, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?
Blinded, he was led into the city, where Ananias baptized him and his sight returned.
In an instant the persecutor became the herald.

The event was so decisive that Paul returns to it again and again in his letters as the pattern of grace: God had chosen him before he was born and called him by grace to preach among the Gentiles the faith he had once tried to destroy.
Apostle to the Gentiles
After years of preparation Paul became the tireless missionary of the early Church, carrying the Gospel across the Roman world on three great journeys.

His labours are recorded in the Acts of the Apostles and confirmed by his own letters: into Cyprus and the cities of Asia Minor across the Aegean into Greece — Philippi, Thessalonica, Corinth, and Athens, where he preached at the Areopagus through Ephesus and back to Jerusalem Everywhere he founded churches and appointed elders, enduring shipwreck, scourging, imprisonment, and stoning for the sake of the Gospel.
The Epistles
Thirteen letters bearing Paul's name stand in the New Testament, addressed to the churches he founded or hoped to visit, and they form the earliest and richest body of Christian theology.

In them he unfolds the doctrine of justification by grace through faith working in love, the unity of Jew and Gentile in one Body of Christ, the meaning of the Cross and Resurrection, and the demands of charity.
His thought has shaped every later age of the Church, from Augustine to the councils, and his phrase in Christ recurs like a refrain through all he wrote.
Prisoner for Christ
A large part of Paul's correspondence was written from prison.

The letters to the Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, and Philemon are traditionally called the captivity epistles , and the pastoral letters to Timothy and Titus give a bishop's counsel on the ordering of the churches and the guarding of sound doctrine.
Even in chains his tone is one of joy: to the Philippians he writes that for him to live is Christ and to die is gain, and bids them rejoice in the Lord always.
His imprisonment became, as he said, a means of spreading the Gospel, so that his bonds were known even in the household of Caesar.
Imprisonment and Martyrdom
Arrested in Jerusalem and held at Caesarea, Paul used his citizenship to appeal to Caesar, and so was sent under guard to Rome , where the Acts leaves him preaching under house arrest.
Tradition holds that he was released, travelled further, and was arrested a second time.

In the persecution under Nero , about the year 64–67, he was martyred — beheaded, as befitted a Roman citizen, by tradition at the place now called Tre Fontane, and buried on the Ostian Way beneath the basilica of St.
Paul Outside the Walls.
Legacy
With St.
Peter , Paul is celebrated on June 29 , and the two are honoured together as the founders of the Roman Church, watered by their blood.
He is often called simply the Apostle.
Christian art shows him with a book or scroll and a sword — the sword both of his martyrdom and of the word of God, which he called sharper than any two-edged blade.
No man save the Lord himself has left so deep a mark on Christian doctrine and devotion.
